segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when we could bear it no longer, we decided to be left behind in Athens alone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the good news of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one would be shaken amid these afflictions. For you yourselves know that this is what we are appointed for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, when we were with you, we kept telling you in advance that we were going to suffer affliction, and so it happened, as you know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why, when I too could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and our labor would turn out to be for nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But just now Timothy has come to us from you and brought us the good news of your faith and love. He has told us that you always remember us fondly and long to see us, just as we long to see you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Because of this, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and affliction we were encouraged about you through your faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for now we live, if you are standing firm in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what thanks can we give back to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as night and day we pray with the utmost earnestness to see your face and to make good what is lacking in your faith?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as for you, may the Lord make you increase and overflow in love for one another and for everyone, just as we do for you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so as to strengthen your hearts to be blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.

notes.note: The Greek 'we' and 'alone' are plural. This may be a literary plural meaning Paul by himself (compare 'I sent' in verse 5), or it may include Silvanus, who is named with Paul as a sender of the letter. Scholars are divided, and the translation keeps the plural without deciding.

notes.traditional: minister of God / our fellow labourer
notes.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read 'God's servant', some simply 'coworker', and some combine the two. Most scholars think 'God's coworker' is original and that copyists softened a phrase that seemed too bold. It can mean one who works alongside God or a colleague of Paul's in God's service; 1 Corinthians 3:9 uses the same expression.

The traditional 'gospel' has become a religious term, but the Greek word was the ordinary one for an announcement of good news, such as a victory. Rendering it this way also preserves a link with verse 6, where Paul uses the related verb, elsewhere his word for proclaiming the message about Christ, for Timothy's good report about the Thessalonians. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. Its older sense is of a dog wagging its tail, and from that 'to fawn on' or 'to beguile', so some take the meaning to be 'so that no one would be lured away'. Most translators and the ancient versions understand it as 'shaken' or 'unsettled', which is followed here.

notes.phrase: the tempter had somehow tempted you
notes.note: The Greek verb covers both 'tempt' and 'put to the test', and the title and the verb are the same word. Here the testing is the pressure of persecution, which might lead the Thessalonians to abandon their faith. 'The tempter' is Satan, named in 2:18.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. 'Brothers' alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The verb is singular in Greek although it has two subjects, God the Father and the Lord Jesus. Greek sometimes lets a verb agree with only one of a pair of subjects, so the grammar alone proves little. Many interpreters nonetheless note how closely Paul joins the two in a single prayer. The verb means to make a road straight, answering the obstruction mentioned in 2:18.
The Greek word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Paul uses it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord.

'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the Greek simply means those who are holy, set apart for God. Paul normally uses it of believers, but here many scholars think he means angels accompanying the Lord, echoing Zechariah 14:5 ('the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him'). 'Holy ones' leaves both readings open.

Some important manuscripts add 'Amen' at the end of this verse. The edition translated here omits it, judging it more likely that copyists added the word to a prayer than that they removed it. The question remains open.

candidates.reason: Very frequent across the New Testament, and translators split between 'gospel' and 'good news'; the choice should be uniform and match the rendering of the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι.
Recurs widely with the verb θλίβω and is variously rendered affliction, tribulation, trouble, suffering or persecution, so readers lose the thread without one decision.
The plural address to congregations occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and inclusive versus traditional 'brothers' must be settled once.
The verb and its noun πειρασμός span 'tempt' and 'test' across the Gospels and the letters, and the choice affects passages such as the Lord's Prayer and the wilderness narratives.
Extremely common and ranges over encourage, comfort, urge and appeal; a sense-by-sense policy is needed so the English does not vary arbitrarily.
